chapterTitle: The Tongue and the Two Wisdoms
themeTitle: “The Wisdom That Is from Above Is First Pure, Then Peaceful”

scripture.text: Let not many of you be teachers, my brothers, knowing that we will receive heavier judgment.
scripture.understanding: μὴ πολλοὶ διδάσκαλοι γίνεσθε, “Let not many of you be teachers” — διδάσκαλος, a recognised teacher of the church, a rabbi. Teaching was honoured and many wanted it. James includes himself — “we will receive heavier judgment” — κρίμα, a verdict. Teachers work with words, and words are the hardest thing to control; the more you say about God, the more you will answer for.

scripture.text: For in many things we all stumble. If anyone doesn’t stumble in word, the same is a perfect man, able to bridle the whole body also.
scripture.understanding: πολλὰ γὰρ πταίομεν ἅπαντες, “For in many things we all stumble” — πταίω, the stumble of 2:10. James puts himself among the stumblers. “If anyone doesn’t stumble in word” — λόγος, from the word family: here simply what you say. “the same is a perfect man” — τέλειος, from the perfect family, as in 1:4: mature, complete. “able to bridle the whole body also” — χαλιναγωγέω, the bridling of 1:26. Control the tongue and you can control everything.

scripture.text: Indeed, we put bits into the horses’ mouths so that they may obey us, and we guide their whole body.
scripture.understanding: “we put bits into the horses’ mouths so that they may obey us” — χαλινός, the bit and bridle. A tiny piece of metal in the mouth turns a powerful animal. μετάγω, to steer, to turn: “and we guide their whole body.” What steers the mouth steers the life.

scripture.text: Behold, the ships also, though they are so big and are driven by fierce winds, are yet guided by a very small rudder, wherever the pilot desires.
scripture.understanding: “Behold, the ships also, though they are so big and are driven by fierce winds” — σκληρός, harsh, rough; ἐλαύνω, pushed along. “are yet guided by a very small rudder” — ἐλάχιστος, the smallest; πηδάλιον, the steering oar. “wherever the pilot desires” — ὁ εὐθύνων, the one who steers straight, and βούλομαι, his will. The tongue is small but it sets the direction, and someone's will is always on the rudder.

scripture.text: So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!
scripture.understanding: “So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things” — μέλος, a part of the body; μεγαλαυχέω, to talk big. Then the image changes from steering to burning: “See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!” — ὕλη, woodland, brushwood; ἀνάπτω, to set alight. In the dry hills of Palestine one spark could consume a valley.

scripture.text: And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.
scripture.understanding: “And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue” — ὁ κόσμος τῆς ἀδικίας. κόσμος, from the world family: the whole system of a fallen world, concentrated in one small organ. ἀδικία, from the sin family: unrighteousness, wrong. “which defiles the whole body” — σπιλόω, to stain, the opposite of the ‘unstained’ life of 1:27. “and sets on fire the course of nature” — τὸν τροχὸν τῆς γενέσεως, ‘the wheel of birth’, the whole cycle of life from birth to death. “and is set on fire by Gehenna” — γέεννα, the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a burning rubbish dump and the picture Jesus used for hell. The tongue's fire is lit from below.

scripture.text: For every kind of animal, bird, creeping thing, and sea creature, is tamed, and has been tamed by mankind;
scripture.understanding: “For every kind of animal, bird, creeping thing, and sea creature, is tamed, and has been tamed by mankind” — the four groups of Genesis 1:26, over which God gave humans dominion. φύσις, nature or kind; δαμάζω, to tame, used twice for emphasis; τῇ φύσει τῇ ἀνθρωπίνῃ, ‘by human nature’. Humanity has tamed lions and elephants.

scripture.text: but nobody can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
scripture.understanding: “but nobody can tame the tongue” — not ‘nobody does’ but ‘nobody can’: no human can do it alone. ἀκατάστατον κακόν, “It is a restless evil” — ἀκατάστατος, the same word as the ‘unstable’ double-minded man (1:8): never at rest. κακός, from the evil family: evil in its very nature. μεστὴ ἰοῦ θανατηφόρου, “full of deadly poison” — ἰός, venom, as of a snake (the same word is ‘rust’ in 5:3).

scripture.text: With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men, who are made in the image of God.
scripture.understanding: ἐν αὐτῇ εὐλογοῦμεν τὸν κύριον καὶ πατέρα, “With it we bless our God and Father” — εὐλογέω, to speak well of. “and with it we curse men” — καταράομαι, to call down evil on someone. “who are made in the image of God” — καθ᾽ ὁμοίωσιν θεοῦ, ‘according to the likeness of God’. ὁμοίωσις, from the image family, is the word of Genesis 1:26 in the Greek Old Testament: ‘in our image (εἰκών), after our likeness (ὁμοίωσις)’. To curse a person is to curse the likeness of the God you have just blessed.

scripture.text: Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.
scripture.understanding: “Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing.” εὐλογία and κατάρα, praise and imprecation. “My brothers, these things ought not to be so” — χρή, it is fitting, it must be; the only use of this word in the New Testament. James does not say ‘this is understandable’. He says it must not be.

scripture.text: Does a spring send out from the same opening fresh and bitter water?
scripture.understanding: “Does a spring send out from the same opening fresh and bitter water?” — πηγή, a spring; ὀπή, its opening in the rock; βρύω, to gush out; γλυκύς, sweet; πικρός, bitter, brackish. In a dry land everyone knew their springs, and no spring gave both.

scripture.text: Can a fig tree, my brothers, yield olives, or a vine figs? Thus no spring yields both salt water and fresh water.
scripture.understanding: “Can a fig tree, my brothers, yield olives, or a vine figs?” — συκῆ, ἐλαία, ἄμπελος, the three great crops of Israel. What a tree is determines what it produces. “Thus no spring yields both salt water and fresh water” — ἁλυκός, salty. Speech reveals the source; Jesus said, ‘By their fruits you will know them.’

scripture.text: Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show by his good conduct that his deeds are done in gentleness of wisdom.
scripture.understanding: τίς σοφὸς καὶ ἐπιστήμων ἐν ὑμῖν, “Who is wise and understanding among you?” — two words from the wisdom family: σοφός, wise in God's ways, and ἐπιστήμων, the knowledgeable expert. This links back to verse 1: those who want to teach. “Let him show by his good conduct” — δείκνυμι, the ‘show me’ of 2:18; καλός, from the good family: fine, attractive conduct; ἀναστροφή, way of life. “that his deeds are done in gentleness of wisdom” — ἔργα, from the work family, and πραΰτης, from the humble family: meekness, the humility of 1:21. Wisdom, like faith, is proved by works.

scripture.text: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart, don’t boast and don’t lie against the truth.
scripture.understanding: “But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart” — ζῆλος πικρός, bitter zeal: the heat of rivalry, the same ‘bitter’ as the spring of verse 11. ἐριθεία, originally a hired worker's self-seeking, then party spirit and selfish ambition. “don’t boast and don’t lie against the truth” — κατακαυχάομαι, the word used in 2:13 of mercy triumphing, here of pride boasting; ψεύδομαι, to lie. Claiming wisdom while nursing rivalry is a lie against the truth.

scripture.text: This wisdom is not that which comes down from above, but is earthly, sensual, and demonic.
scripture.understanding: “This wisdom is not that which comes down from above” — σοφία, from the wisdom family, but ἄνωθεν κατερχομένη, the language of 1:17, where every good gift comes down from above. This wisdom has another source. Three steps downward: ἐπίγειος, “earthly” — belonging to this world; ψυχικός, “sensual” — natural, unspiritual, the life of the soul without the Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:14); δαιμονιώδης, “demonic” — demon-like, and demon-inspired. Clever, but from below.

scripture.text: For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed.
scripture.understanding: “For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed.” ἀκαταστασία, disorder, upheaval — the noun of the ‘unstable’ (1:8) and ‘restless’ (3:8). φαῦλος, from the evil family: worthless, base, vile — not κακός (evil in nature, v. 8) or πονηρός (actively harmful, 2:4), but cheap and shoddy evil. πρᾶγμα, a deed, a practice.

scripture.text: But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
scripture.understanding: “But the wisdom that is from above is first pure” — σοφία, from the wisdom family; ἁγνός, clean, free from mixture. πρῶτον, first: purity before everything. Then seven qualities: εἰρηνική, “peaceful”; ἐπιεικής, “gentle” — reasonable, yielding, not insisting on one's rights; εὐπειθής, “reasonable” — easy to persuade, open to correction; μεστὴ ἐλέους καὶ καρπῶν ἀγαθῶν, “full of mercy and good fruits” — ἔλεος, from the mercy family; ἀγαθός, from the good family: good in its usefulness, compared with the καλός of verse 13; ἀδιάκριτος, “without partiality” — undivided, from the same root as the doubter (1:6) and the favouritism (2:4); ἀνυπόκριτος, “without hypocrisy” — sincere, not playing a part. It reads like a portrait of Jesus.

scripture.text: Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.
scripture.understanding: “Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” καρπὸς δικαιοσύνης, the harvest that righteousness produces; σπείρω, to sow. Peacemakers sow in peace, and they reap righteous lives — their own and others'. Jesus called them blessed and children of God.

visualMeditations.title: The Bit and the Rudder
visualMeditations.image: Picture a war horse, strong enough to kill a man with one kick, standing quietly while a rider turns it left and right with a small strip of metal in its mouth. Then picture a cargo ship in a storm, waves breaking over its bow, wind roaring in its sails — and at the back a single sailor leaning on a narrow wooden oar, keeping the whole vessel on course.
visualMeditations.meaning: “Indeed, we put bits into the horses’ mouths so that they may obey us, and we guide their whole body” (v. 3). “Behold, the ships also, though they are so big and are driven by fierce winds, are yet guided by a very small rudder, wherever the pilot desires” (v. 4). Your tongue is small, but it is steering your life — your relationships, your reputation, your witness, your future. The question is not whether your life is being steered, but whose hand is on the rudder.

visualMeditations.title: The Forest Fire
visualMeditations.image: Picture a dry hillside at the end of summer, the grass brown and brittle. A traveller drops a single glowing ember. A thread of smoke rises, then a small flame, then the wind catches it. Within an hour the whole valley is burning, villages are fleeing, and the sky is black with smoke. All of it from one spark.
visualMeditations.meaning: “See how a small fire can spread to a large forest! And the tongue is a fire” (vv. 5–6). One rumour can destroy a reputation; one careless sentence can split a church; one cruel word can scar a child for life. And James says the fire is “set on fire by Gehenna” (v. 6) — the enemy loves to light it. Before you speak, ask what you are about to set alight.

visualMeditations.title: The Two Springs
visualMeditations.image: Picture a traveller in the desert reaching a spring. He kneels and drinks — and the water is sweet. The next day he comes back to the same spring and drinks again — and it is bitter, salty, undrinkable. He would never trust that spring again. Then picture a believer in church singing praise with tears, and in the car park afterwards cursing another driver.
visualMeditations.meaning: “With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men, who are made in the image of God” (v. 9). “Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so” (v. 10). The mouth reveals the spring. If bitter water flows, there is bitterness at the source. The answer is not just to guard the mouth but to have the spring itself made new.

visualMeditations.title: Two Gardens of Wisdom
visualMeditations.image: Picture two gardens side by side. In the first, everything is competition: every plant grows tall by choking its neighbours, thorns spread, and the ground is torn up by roots fighting for space. In the second, the plants are watered, pruned and spaced; fruit hangs heavy on the branches; and the gardener moves quietly among them, planting seeds in calm soil.
visualMeditations.meaning: “For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed” (v. 16). “But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy” (v. 17). “Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace” (v. 18). You can tell which wisdom is ruling a person — or a church — by the garden it produces.

structure.label: A Warning to Teachers (v. 1-2)
structure.body: Not many should become teachers, since teachers will be judged more strictly; we all stumble in many ways, and whoever does not stumble in speech is mature and able to bridle the whole body.

structure.label: The Power of the Tongue (v. 3-6)
structure.body: Like a bit in a horse's mouth or a rudder on a ship, the small tongue directs the whole; like a spark it can set a forest alight; it is a fire, a world of unrighteousness, staining the body and inflamed by hell.

structure.label: The Untameable Tongue (v. 7-12)
structure.body: Every kind of creature has been tamed, but no human can tame the tongue, a restless evil full of deadly poison; with it we bless God and curse people made in His likeness; a spring cannot give both sweet and bitter water, nor a fig tree olives.

structure.label: Two Kinds of Wisdom (v. 13-18)
structure.body: The wise person shows wisdom by good conduct done in meekness; bitter jealousy and selfish ambition reveal a wisdom that is earthly, unspiritual and demonic, producing disorder and evil; the wisdom from above is pure, peaceful, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere, and peacemakers sow a harvest of righteousness.

sections.heading: Small Member, Great Power
paragraphs: James has already mentioned the tongue twice: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak” (James 1:19), and “If anyone among you thinks himself to be religious while he doesn’t bridle his tongue … this man’s religion is worthless” (James 1:26). Now he gives it a whole chapter. He begins with teachers, because their work is words: “Let not many of you be teachers, my brothers, knowing that we will receive heavier judgment” (v. 1). Jesus said, “I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36). The more you speak in God's name, the more seriously He takes your words.

Then James widens the warning to everyone: “For in many things we all stumble. If anyone doesn’t stumble in word, the same is a perfect man, able to bridle the whole body also” (v. 2). The tongue is the test of maturity. It is the last thing to be brought under control, and once it is controlled, everything else follows. That is the point of the bit and the rudder (vv. 3–4): small things steer great things. A few words at the right moment can turn a life towards God; a few words at the wrong moment can wreck it.

The tongue also destroys. “And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna” (v. 6). That is one of the strongest sentences in the New Testament. James says the tongue carries the whole fallen world-system inside it — all the pride, lust, greed and hatred of a world without God — and it can stain your whole life from birth to death. Its fire is lit from hell itself. Gossip, slander, lies, flattery, harshness and boasting are not small sins. They are fires.

sections.heading: No One Can Tame It — but God Can Change the Spring
paragraphs: James's honesty is startling: “but nobody can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison” (v. 8). Humanity has tamed every kind of creature — beasts, birds, reptiles and sea creatures (v. 7) — but not its own mouth. Paul, quoting the Psalms, describes the human condition in the same terms: “Their throat is an open tomb. With their tongues they have used deceit” (Romans 3:13), “whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness” (Romans 3:14). No self-help programme can fully master the tongue.

Why not? Because the tongue is not the source of the problem; it is the outlet. Jesus said, “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34), and “But the things which proceed out of the mouth come out of the heart, and they defile the man” (Matthew 15:18). That is why James moves to the spring and the tree (vv. 11–12). A spring gives the water that is in it; a fig tree gives figs. If cursing flows from the same mouth that blesses God, the problem is a divided heart — the double-mindedness of 1:8 again.

So James is not driving us to despair but to God. No human can tame the tongue, but God can make a new heart, and a new heart produces new speech. At Pentecost the Holy Spirit came as “Tongues like fire” (Acts 2:3) — heaven's fire answering hell's fire — and the disciples' tongues were filled with the praises of God. Paul gives the positive rule: “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). The cure for a poisoned tongue is a cleansed spring, a Spirit-filled heart, and the daily practice of being “swift to hear, slow to speak” (James 1:19).

sections.heading: Two Wisdoms, Two Harvests
paragraphs: Verse 13 returns to those who want to teach: “Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show by his good conduct that his deeds are done in gentleness of wisdom.” As with faith in chapter 2, James insists that wisdom must be shown. Wisdom is not how much you know, how well you argue or how impressively you speak. It is how you live — and especially whether you live with meekness.

There is a false wisdom, and James describes it without mercy. Its roots are “bitter jealousy and selfish ambition” (v. 14). It may be clever, persuasive and successful, but its source is “earthly, sensual, and demonic” (v. 15) — it belongs to this world, it is driven by natural desires rather than the Spirit, and it is inspired by the devil. Its fruit is visible: “confusion and every evil deed” (v. 16). Paul lists the same things among the works of the flesh: “hatred, strife, jealousies, outbursts of anger, rivalries, divisions” (Galatians 5:20). Whenever a church is torn by rivalry, someone's wisdom is from below.

The true wisdom comes down from above, like every good and perfect gift (1:17), and it is the answer to the prayer of 1:5. James describes it in eight qualities: pure, peaceful, gentle, reasonable, merciful, fruitful, impartial and sincere (v. 17). It is strikingly close to Paul's fruit of the Spirit: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith” (Galatians 5:22), “gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:23). And it is a portrait of Christ Himself, who “was made to us wisdom from God” (1 Corinthians 1:30). Its harvest is righteousness, sown by peacemakers (v. 18). Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9).

ntConnection.heading: Words, Fruit, and the Wisdom of Christ
paragraphs: James's teaching on the tongue is Jesus' teaching. Jesus said, “For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Matthew 12:37). He taught that a tree is known by its fruit: “By their fruits you will know them. Do you gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” (Matthew 7:16), and “Even so, every good tree produces good fruit; but the corrupt tree produces evil fruit” (Matthew 7:17). James's fig tree that cannot produce olives (v. 12) is the same lesson. Peter, who knew the tongue's dangers from bitter experience, quotes Psalm 34: “He who would love life, and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil, and his lips from speaking deceit” (1 Peter 3:10).

The curse on people made in God's likeness (v. 9) reaches back to Genesis 1:26 and forward to the new creation. Paul says the believer “put on the new man, who is being renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator” (Colossians 3:10). To curse another person is to attack the image God is restoring. To bless them is to honour Him.

Above all, the wisdom from above has a name. Paul writes that “Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), the one “in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden” (Colossians 2:3). Every quality of James 3:17 is fulfilled in Him: pure, peaceful, gentle, open, merciful, fruitful, impartial and sincere. To ask God for wisdom (James 1:5) is ultimately to ask for more of Christ to be formed in you. The fruit of righteousness sown in peace (v. 18) echoes Hebrews: discipline “yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been exercised thereby” (Hebrews 12:11).

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “the tongue; by implication, a language”. James uses it five times, more than any other New Testament letter except 1 Corinthians, where it means languages. In James it is the organ of speech, and it carries a whole world of good and evil. The same word is used at Pentecost for the tongues of fire and for the new languages the Spirit gave. The tongue set on fire by Gehenna (v. 6) can become a tongue set on fire by the Spirit (Acts 2:3–4). What lights your tongue determines what it burns.

Strong's: “valley of (the son of) Hinnom.” The valley south of Jerusalem where kings of Judah once burned their children in sacrifice to Molech, later a place of burning refuse. Jesus used it as the name of hell, the place of final judgement. Outside the Gospels this is the only time it appears in the New Testament. James's point is that the destructive fire of the tongue has its source in the realm of evil itself. Gossip and slander are not merely human failings; they serve the enemy's purposes.

Strong's: “assimilation, i.e. resemblance.” ὁμοίωσις is the word the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 1:26, ‘after our likeness’. The WEB translates it ‘image’ here. It differs from εἰκών, the image or representation itself, by stressing resemblance. This study adds it to the image family. Every human being still bears God's likeness, even after the fall. That is why cursing people is so serious: it is an attack on someone who resembles God.

Strong's: “properly, intrigue, i.e. (by implication) faction.” The word once described people who worked for hire and then came to mean those who campaign for themselves — the politics of self-promotion, party spirit and rivalry. It is paired with ζῆλος, which can be good zeal or bad jealousy; here it is ‘bitter’. Together they describe the person who wants to be first, cannot bear another's success, and gathers followers. Paul uses the same word: ‘doing nothing through rivalry’ (Philippians 2:3).

Strong's: “appropriate, i.e. (by implication) mild.” ἐπιεικής is one of the hardest words in the New Testament to translate. It describes someone who does not insist on the letter of their rights, who yields when yielding is right, and who is fair-minded and gracious rather than rigid. Paul uses the noun of ‘the gentleness of Christ’ (2 Corinthians 10:1), and requires it of overseers (1 Timothy 3:3). It is the mark of wisdom that does not need to win every argument.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: In this chapter the Holy Spirit is putting His finger on your mouth — and tracing what comes out of it back to your heart.

items.title: What Is Steering Your Life?
items.body: Your words are a rudder. The Spirit wants you to see where they have been steering you — towards peace or conflict, towards faith or fear, towards love or bitterness. Listen to yourself for a day. What are you saying about God, about yourself, about others, about your future? “If anyone doesn’t stumble in word, the same is a perfect man, able to bridle the whole body also” (v. 2). What would change if your words were in His hands?

items.title: Put Out the Fire
items.body: Is there a fire burning because of something you said — a rumour you passed on, a harsh word, a careless criticism, a lie? “See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!” (v. 5). The Spirit is not condemning you; He is calling you to put it out. That may mean going back to someone and apologising, correcting what you said, or simply stopping a conversation. Which fire does He want you to deal with first?

items.title: Which Wisdom Are You Using?
items.body: In the decisions you are making — at work, in ministry, in your family — are you driven by “bitter jealousy and selfish ambition” (v. 14), or by the wisdom that is “first pure, then peaceful” (v. 17)? Selfish ambition can wear religious clothes. Ask the Spirit to show you where you are competing instead of serving, and to give you the wisdom that comes down from above.

audit.title: The Spark Check
audit.body: Have your words started any fires this month — gossip, sarcasm, complaint, harsh criticism (vv. 5–6)? Name one conversation where you should have stayed silent.

audit.title: The Spring Check
audit.body: Does the same mouth that praises God on Sunday curse, mock or belittle people during the week (vv. 9–10)? Who do you speak about in ways you would never speak about God?

audit.title: The Ambition Check
audit.body: Is there anyone whose success you find hard to celebrate (v. 14)? Where are you pushing for position, recognition or control? Measure your wisdom against the eight qualities of verse 17.

practices.title: A Day of Guarded Speech
practices.body: Choose one full day this week. Before you speak in any conversation, ask three silent questions: Is it true? Is it necessary? Is it kind and building up (Ephesians 4:29)? If the answer to any is no, stay silent or change your words. In the evening, write down what you noticed about your tongue and pray verse 2 over yourself.

practices.title: Bless Those You Have Cursed
practices.body: Think of someone you have criticised, mocked or spoken against. This week, deliberately speak a blessing over them: pray for them by name, thank God for His likeness in them, and if possible say something genuinely encouraging to them or about them to others. Replace the bitter water with sweet.

prayerReflection: “Father, I bless You with my mouth, and I confess that with the same mouth I have spoken against people made in Your likeness. Forgive me. These things ought not to be so. I admit that I cannot tame my tongue by my own strength; it is restless and quick to spark fires. So I ask You to change the spring. Make my heart pure, so that what flows from my mouth is sweet and not bitter. Put Your bit in my mouth and take hold of the rudder of my life. Where my words have set fires, give me courage to put them out. Holy Spirit, set my tongue on fire with heaven's fire, as You did at Pentecost, so that I speak words of grace that build others up. Deliver me from bitter jealousy and selfish ambition, and from every wisdom that is earthly, unspiritual and demonic. Give me the wisdom that comes down from above — pure, peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality and without hypocrisy. Make me a peacemaker who sows in peace and reaps a harvest of righteousness. In Jesus' name, Amen.”

storyConnections.title: Peter's Tongue in the Courtyard
storyConnections.summary: Peter, who had boasted that he would never deny Jesus, warmed himself by a fire in the high priest's courtyard while his Lord was on trial. A servant girl said, ‘You were with Jesus.’ Peter denied it. Another said the same, and he denied it with an oath. Finally, when people recognised his accent, “Then he began to curse and to swear, ‘I don’t know the man!’ Immediately the rooster crowed” (Matthew 26:74). The same mouth that had confessed ‘You are the Christ’ now cursed. Peter went out and wept bitterly. Yet after the resurrection the same tongue preached at Pentecost and three thousand were saved. The tongue nobody can tame was transformed by the Spirit.

storyConnections.title: Tongues Like Fire
storyConnections.summary: On the day of Pentecost the disciples were gathered together when a sound like a rushing wind filled the house. “Tongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them, and one sat on each of them” (Acts 2:3). “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak” (Acts 2:4). James says the tongue is a fire set alight by hell; at Pentecost God set tongues alight with heaven's fire. The result was not destruction but praise, preaching and a harvest of three thousand. The same organ that spreads destruction can, under the Spirit, spread the gospel.

storyConnections.title: The Sons of Thunder Want Fire
storyConnections.summary: When a Samaritan village refused to welcome Jesus, two disciples — James the son of Zebedee (not the writer of this letter) and his brother John — were furious. “Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from the sky, and destroy them, just as Elijah did?” (Luke 9:54). Jesus nicknamed them Boanerges, ‘Sons of Thunder’. “But he turned and rebuked them” (Luke 9:55). Their zeal sounded biblical, but it was bitter and proud. Jesus simply went to another village. It is a picture of the two wisdoms: one that wants to call down fire, and one that is peaceable, gentle and full of mercy. John, the Son of Thunder, later became the apostle of love.
